cells.tense: You are the one deciding what stays and what gets let go, and the deciding is steady.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're keeping only out of habit, and say out loud what it would cost to release it.
cells.core:
You know what to keep and what to let go. Not by calculation — by a feel for it that shows up in the small choices: what you hold onto, what you pass on, what you quietly stop maintaining. That sense runs underneath what you're doing.

And the choices that land tend to be fair, and people feel that, because you're not keeping score while you make them. That's the whole trick — the exchange stays open instead of turning into a ledger. So the ground stays fertile without you having to turn it by hand. You can trust the read enough to move on it.
cells.sheetLine: You know what to release, and releasing keeps the ground open.
cells.verb: Transforming what's held into ground for what comes next

cells.tense: You will be bracing for the ending that hasn't come yet, and treating it as already overdue.
cells.ask: Name one ending you're preparing for, and ask the person involved whether it's actually ending.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the ending. Somewhere in you the ending has already happened, and you're living past it — deciding what to cut, what to clear out, what to rebuild — while the thing itself is untouched. The bracing is costing you the contact you'd need to close it well.

You don't have to feel your way through this alone, either. That's the part you skip when you move fast: the person on the other side of the change is someone to reach, not a variable to manage. Reach them before you act, and you'll find out which endings are real. The ones that are will go better.

cells.tense: You stood at a door that's already closed behind you and you are still facing it.
cells.ask: Do one small thing today that you'd do if the change were already over — an email, a shelf cleared, a call.
cells.core:
Ending something cleanly is available to you, and when it happens the release feeds what comes next — one thing lets go, the next thing has room, nothing has to be argued for or defended. The reach toward what's ahead shows up as its own kind of direction, and the exchange around you keeps moving because you keep it honest.

Right now something needs to move and you've stopped moving it. The reach toward it stopped somewhere, and the stopped place has been setting the pace. Meanwhile the thing keeps sitting there, untouched and unaddressed. An idea about what to do isn't what's absent. It's the first reach, done badly, with no guarantee attached. Pick the smallest move you can make today and make it before you talk yourself out of it. Direction arrives after you're already in motion. Put the effort into the motion itself.

cells.tense: You are already recalibrating what's out of proportion, and you are describing yourself as just getting through it.
cells.ask: Say 'I'm the one who set this right' about one thing that's currently in order because you arranged it.
cells.core:
The balance you keep landing on didn't happen on its own. When things get out of proportion around you, you're the one who adjusts them — a conversation brought up, a decision made, a clear line drawn that lets people stop guessing. It happens quietly and often enough to be easy to miss.

The way you speak of it, the circumstances did the work — not you. The willingness is real, and the effect on the people around you is real, and you haven't put your name on it. That's the gap worth closing: what you call just getting through it is the thing you are actually doing in the room. Say so, at least to yourself.
